The "claw sign" (renal parenchyma wrapping around the mass) tells you that the mass arises from the kidney. A solid renal mass without macroscopic fat should be considered malignant until proven otherwise, even in young people.
Differential diagnosis of solid renal masses without fat: clear cell carcinoma is hypervascular and heterogeneous (necrosis); papillary is hypovascular and homogeneous (weak and slow enhancement, often < 20-30 HU); chromophobe has intermediate, homogeneous enhancement, sometimes a central scar like oncocytoma, from which it cannot be distinguished on imaging; lipid-poor angiomyolipoma is often hyperdense on unenhanced images. Infiltrative lesions that preserve the shape of the kidney suggest urothelial carcinoma, lymphoma, metastasis or pyelonephritis, not a typical renal carcinoma.
With a single phase enhancement cannot be measured: in a real case it is completed with the unenhanced phase (and MRI if needed). Management of solid masses is surgical; in small tumors (T1) partial nephrectomy is preferred to preserve renal function.
